chapter.title: Replication
chapter.author: Martin Kleppmann
chapter.primary_goal: Understand single-leader, multi-leader, and leaderless replication; the effects of replication lag; quorum behavior; and how distributed systems reason about concurrent writes and conflict resolution.

summary.overview: Replication keeps copies of changing data on several machines to improve availability, latency, disconnected operation, and read scalability. The central difficulty is coordinating changes while machines fail, networks delay messages, followers lag, and multiple clients write concurrently. Single-leader systems route all writes through one leader and replicate to followers, making ordering relatively easy but introducing failover and lag concerns. Multi-leader systems allow several leaders to accept writes, which is useful across datacenters, offline clients, and collaborative editing but requires conflict resolution. Leaderless/Dynamo-style systems write and read from several replicas directly, using quorums, read repair, anti-entropy, sloppy quorums, hinted handoff, siblings, tombstones, and version vectors. The chapter also develops read-your-writes, monotonic reads, consistent-prefix reads, happens-before causality, and the distinction between causally ordered and concurrent writes.

single_leader.definition: One leader accepts writes; followers replay the leader's change stream. Reads can use leader or followers.

sync_vs_async.synchronous: Leader waits for follower acknowledgement before reporting success.
sync_vs_async.asynchronous: Leader does not wait; follower may lag and acknowledged writes may be lost if leader dies before replication.
sync_vs_async.semi_synchronous: Commonly one synchronous follower and other followers asynchronous.

new_follower: Record the snapshot's exact replication-log position.
Replay all changes since that position.
single_leader.follower_failure: Catch-up recovery from the last processed log position.
single_leader.leader_failure: Failover: detect failure, elect/promote a new leader, reroute clients/followers, and demote the old leader if it returns.
failover_risks: Loss of asynchronously replicated acknowledged writes

wal_shipping.tradeoff: Efficient but tightly coupled to storage-engine format and often software version.

logical_log.idea: Replicate row-level logical inserts, deletes, updates, and commit markers.

trigger_based.idea: Use triggers/stored procedures plus external application logic.
trigger_based.tradeoff: Flexible but generally higher overhead and more error-prone.

replication_lag_and_consistency.eventual_consistency: If writes stop and enough time passes, asynchronous followers eventually catch up.
replication_lag_and_consistency.replication_lag: Delay between the leader applying a write and a follower applying it.
replication_lag_and_consistency.read_after_write: A user always sees their own writes.
replication_lag_and_consistency.monotonic_reads: A user never sees an older version after previously seeing a newer one.
replication_lag_and_consistency.consistent_prefix_reads: Causally ordered writes are observed in that same order.
read_after_write_techniques: Route recent post-write reads to leader
Track the user's latest logical write position and require a replica at least that current

multi_leader.definition: Several leaders accept writes and asynchronously replicate changes to one another.
multi_leader.conflict_avoidance: Route all writes for one logical record/user to the same leader where possible.
multi_leader.convergence_requirement: All replicas must eventually reach the same state after receiving all changes.
conflict_resolution: Preserve all conflicting versions for later resolution
multi_leader.topology_tradeoff: Sparse topologies can be interrupted by a failed intermediate node; all-to-all is more fault-tolerant but can reorder causally related messages.

leaderless.definition: Any replica can accept writes; clients/coordinators write to several replicas and read from several replicas.
leaderless.read_repair: A multi-replica read detects stale values and writes the newer value back.
leaderless.anti_entropy: Background process compares replicas and copies missing data.

quorum.n: Number of replicas for a value

examples.effect: Fast reads but one failed replica blocks writes

quorum_limits: Sloppy quorums may destroy strict read/write-set overlap.
Concurrent writes have no inherent total order.
Reads racing writes may return old or new values.
Failed writes may remain on replicas where they succeeded.
Recovery from stale replicas can reduce copies of the newest value.
Timing edge cases can still produce stale reads.
leaderless.sloppy_quorum: Use reachable non-home nodes to satisfy w/r for greater availability.
leaderless.hinted_handoff: Temporary nodes later forward accepted writes to the proper home replicas.

concurrency.last_write_wins: Use an arbitrary ordering, often timestamps, and discard all but the winning value; convergent but can lose data.
concurrency.happens_before: A happens before B if B knows about, depends on, or builds on A.
concurrency.concurrent: Two operations are concurrent if neither happens before the other.
concurrency.physical_time_note: Concurrency is about causality, not literal simultaneity.
concurrency.siblings: Concurrent versions preserved for application merge.
concurrency.tombstone: Versioned deletion marker needed so removals are not resurrected during merges.
concurrency.version_vector: Per-replica version state for a key that distinguishes overwrites from concurrent writes.
concurrency.vector_clock_note: Version vectors and vector clocks are related but not identical; the chapter says version vectors are appropriate for comparing replica state.

short_answer_questions.question: Compare synchronous and asynchronous replication.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Synchronous waits for follower acknowledgement, improving durability but risking write unavailability. Asynchronous does not wait, improving latency/availability but risking acknowledged write loss after leader failure.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is failover difficult?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Failure detection is uncertain, candidates may be stale, writes may be lost, split brain may occur, and timeout choices trade false failover against slow recovery.

short_answer_questions.question: Compare statement, WAL, logical, and trigger replication.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Statement replication replays commands but struggles with nondeterminism; WAL shipping is physical and version-coupled; logical logs are row-level and evolvable; triggers are flexible but application-driven and higher overhead.

short_answer_questions.question: Compare read-your-writes, monotonic reads, and consistent-prefix reads.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Read-your-writes preserves a user's own updates; monotonic reads prevent backward movement in observed state; consistent prefix preserves causal order.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is multi-leader useful across datacenters?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Writes can be local and continue through WAN/datacenter failures, but concurrent writes create conflicts.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is LWW risky?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: It forces an arbitrary order and discards losing writes, even if they were successfully acknowledged.

short_answer_questions.question: How does leaderless replication work during node failure?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Writes go to several replicas and wait for w; reads query several and wait for r. Read repair and anti-entropy repair stale nodes without leader failover.

short_answer_questions.question: What does w+r>n mean?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Under strict quorum assumptions, the read and successful write sets overlap in at least one replica.

short_answer_questions.question: Why isn't quorum overlap strong consistency?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Sloppy quorums, concurrent writes, read/write races, partial failed writes, stale recovery, and timing edge cases can still produce stale or ambiguous values.

short_answer_questions.question: What are sloppy quorum and hinted handoff?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Sloppy quorum temporarily stores writes on reachable non-home nodes; hinted handoff later transfers them to home replicas.

short_answer_questions.question: How is concurrency defined?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: By causality: two operations are concurrent when neither happens-before the other, not merely when timestamps overlap.

short_answer_questions.question: Why are version vectors necessary?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: With several write-accepting replicas, per-replica version history is needed to distinguish causal overwrites from concurrent sibling values.

common_confusions.confusion: Replication is the same as partitioning.
common_confusions.correction: Replication copies the same data; partitioning divides data into subsets.
A confirmed write may still be lost if leader dies before replication.

common_confusions.confusion: Eventual consistency means lag is always short.
common_confusions.correction: There is no general upper bound on lag.

common_confusions.confusion: Monotonic reads mean globally fresh data.
common_confusions.correction: They only prevent a single user from moving backward after seeing newer data.

common_confusions.confusion: Multi-leader removes the single-leader bottleneck for free.
common_confusions.correction: It introduces concurrent-write conflicts and causal-ordering issues.
It gives overlap under strict assumptions, but several failure/concurrency cases still permit stale values.

common_confusions.confusion: Sloppy quorum is a traditional strict quorum.
common_confusions.correction: It may use non-home replicas and mainly provides durability/availability until hinted handoff completes.
Concurrency means neither operation causally depends on the other.
The chapter notes a subtle distinction and recommends version vectors for replica-state comparison.

Single-leader = one write leader, followers replay ordered changes.
Sync improves durability but can block writes; async improves availability but risks acknowledged write loss.
Follower bootstrap = snapshot + log position + catch-up.
Failover hazards include stale promotion, write loss, split brain, timeout mistakes.
Statement replication has nondeterminism problems; WAL is physical; logical logs are row-level and CDC-friendly.
Multi-leader is useful for multi-DC/offline/collaboration but requires conflict resolution.
LWW converges by discarding writes and can lose data.
Leaderless uses n replicas, waits for w write acks and r read responses.
Read repair and anti-entropy repair stale replicas.
Sloppy quorum improves availability by using non-home nodes; hinted handoff returns writes home.
Happens-before defines causality; concurrency is neither operation happening before the other.
Siblings preserve concurrent versions; tombstones preserve deletions.
Version vectors track per-replica causal state.
